subject: Insurance is the silent margin killer — quote it BEFORE you offer
preheader: Coastal premiums up 25-40% over 5 yrs · Midwest still stable · The $80-400/mo gap most investors miss

marketSnapshot.headline: Property insurance has reshaped which markets pencil
marketSnapshot.body: Property insurance is the rental-underwriting line item that's moved most in the last 5 years. Coastal markets (FL, LA, Texas coastal, parts of CA fire zones) have repriced 25-40% over that window. Midwest, Northeast, and non-coastal Southeast are mostly stable or up only modestly. The biggest underwriting mistake: using the seller's last-year insurance figure instead of getting a fresh quote in your name. The gap is often $80-150/mo on a single-family rental, $200-400/mo on a 2-4 unit — and that gap can flip a deal from Strong to Marginal.

dealSpotter.body: The classic Florida insurance gotcha. Seller has a legacy policy from a carrier that's no longer writing new policies in the zone. Your new-buyer quote comes back at $7,200/yr — nearly double. A deal that looked like an 8.2% cap re-pencils to 6.1% cap once the real insurance is plugged in. The fix: ALWAYS quote insurance yourself before signing the contract. Don't accept the seller's number.

Cleveland, Indianapolis, Cincinnati, parts of MO/PA — insurance pricing has been mostly stable. A property quoted at $800/yr today is likely to be $850-900/yr in 5 years. The 5-year planning horizon is predictable. This is part of why Midwest cash-flow markets have outperformed coastal markets on underwriting reliability through the 2024-2026 insurance shock.

California has a tier of properties where private carriers have entirely exited and only the state's FAIR Plan will write coverage. FAIR is bare-bones, expensive, and the only option for owners. If the only insurance available for a property is FAIR Plan and the premium runs $4-7k/yr on a single-family, the deal almost never pencils. Run insurance availability as a first-pass filter in CA, not as a final-step check.

blogFeature.title: How to spot a bad rental deal in 60 seconds — 7 red flags
blogFeature.excerpt: Property insurance volatility is one of the 7 red flags. The flag isn't 'high premium' — it's 'premium has been moving fast in the wrong direction and likely to continue.'

qa.question: How do I get a real insurance quote BEFORE I've made an offer on a property?
qa.answer: Two paths. (1) Most insurance brokers will quote a 'prospective' policy if you give them the property address, year built, square footage, roof age, and your intent to use as an investment property. Tell them you're considering an offer and need to know the premium. They'll either quote in a day or two, or tell you they can't write the policy at all (which is also useful information). (2) Use online quote engines (Lemonade, Hippo, State Farm online) for fast directional numbers, but verify with a broker before closing — online quotes for investment properties are often quoted at owner-occupant rates and adjusted later. Always get the quote in writing. Always include 'investment property' / 'tenant occupied' in the application — premiums for tenant-occupied are higher than owner-occupied by 15-30%. If the quote comes back materially different from what the seller represented, that's a price-negotiation lever.
